title: Product Life Extension Strategies: The Shift from Linear Disposal to Circular Design
text:
Historically, product management and urban material flow were structured around the fundamental and rejected assumption of linear resource availability—a model best characterized as 'Take-Make-Dispose.' This foundational paradigm treated natural resources as infinitely replenishable inputs and viewed end-of-life products merely as externalized waste streams that required mitigation through landfills or basic incineration. Within Sustainable Urban Planning, this perspective necessitated purely logistical solutions focused on efficient removal of garbage rather than fundamental changes in product utility.

The failure point of the linear model became acutely apparent with global resource depletion and mounting rates of accumulated solid waste. The early attempts to address material cycling were largely confined to remediation efforts—improving basic recycling infrastructure to handle materials at their single most obvious recovery points (e.g., aluminum cans, glass). However, these methods remained trapped in the logic that simply minimizing disposal volume was equivalent to creating sustainability.

This recognition of insufficiency paved the way for Product Life Extension Strategies within Circular Economy Modeling. The rejected theory shifted from viewing waste as a problem of 'disposal' to understanding it as a failure of systemic design—the failure to retain embedded value. Consequently, modern modeling must transcend simple material recovery by integrating product stewardship and system-level looping, treating maintenance, refurbishment, and resale not as secondary options, but as the primary architectural functions of an urban built environment.
